linguistics.meaning: Bed Springs — descriptive Cree phrase: 'a bed (sleeping-place), the thing(s) that bounce'
linguistics.type: descriptive noun phrase (NI + ka- relative clause + NI plural)

morphemes.gloss: NI noun: 'bed, sleeping place' — from VAI nipâ‑ 'to sleep' + the place/state nominalizer ‑win ('the place/act of sleeping')
relative-clause prefix (shortened conjunct kâ‑ 'the one that…') — introduces the descriptive clause 'that bounces'

II verb (changed conjunct of kwâskwêkotêw): '(the thing) that bounces, that springs, that recoils' — root kwâskw‑ 'jump, bounce' is the same productive initial in kwâskohtin 'it bounces off (involuntarily)' and kwâskwepayiw 'it springs into motion'
INDEF noun, plural: 'things' (animate plural / pejorative-flavoured) — base kîkway 'something, what', with plural marker ‑ak

relatedForms.note: The standalone NI noun appears unchanged inside the headword.

relatedForms.english: It bounces, it springs back, it recoils

morphemes.gloss: II final: '(it) does so by itself; (it) hangs/dangles in that manner'

relatedForms.note: The 'plain' independent form. Changed-conjunct kâ kwâskwêkotêk 'the one that bounces' is what the plaque uses, written as ka kwâskwekotek.
Plural kîkwayak 'things' carries an animate plural — a small grammatical wink, since bedsprings 'jump' and so can be cast as animate.

quickReference.note: Descriptive Cree phrase, not a single lexeme.
II verb. Changed-conjunct = 'kâ kwâskwêkotêk' 'the one that bounces'.

culturalStory.heading: Springs Underfoot
body: The plaque does not name a single Cree word for 'bed-spring' — there isn't one in everyday speech. Instead the carving spells out a small descriptive sentence: nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak, literally 'a bed (a sleeping-place), the thing(s) that bounce.' It is the kind of phrase a Cree speaker might construct on the fly to describe a piece of unfamiliar furniture, and it preserves that exploratory, fitted-to-the-object register on a permanent sign.

The plaque itself is the most three-dimensional in the whole wall: a row of small black metal springs is mounted directly into the white plaque face, with a blue inset panel holding the red Cree syllabics. nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak is carved in black above, with kîkwayak floated in blue to match the panel. Bed Springs sits at the bottom in matching blue. The combination reads as a 'physical pun' — the literal springs sit between the words for 'bed' and 'things that bounce'.

Bed Springs the mountain-bike trail runs through Patricia Ravine on Edmonton's southwest side, black-diamond rated, a short rooty ribbon that earns its name by the way the rooty fall-line section makes a rider's saddle 'sproing' off the pedals. The trail sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory). The neighbouring trail in the same network is, fittingly, called Sproing! — same gag, same family of names.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The carved plaque reads SRO nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak (with circumflexes on ê of nipêwin, â of kwâskwekotek, and î of kîkwayak). The current catalogue.json creeName is kekokel sôniyâwâhkêsis — that is in fact the Cree word for SILVERFOX and was accidentally placed on the Bed Springs entry. Coordinator should set bed-springs creeName to nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak and creeSyllabics to ᓂᐯᐃᐣ ᑲ ᑳᐢᑵᑯᑌᐠ ᑮᑿᔭᐠ.

The form ka kwâskwekotek is the relative / changed-conjunct of the II verb kwâskwêkotêw 'it bounces'. The plaque writes ka (short a) rather than kâ (long â) — both are attested in carved signage; kâ‑ is the standard descriptive-relative prefix. The internal vowels of kwâskwekotek on the plaque are short in places where standard published Cree would write kwâskwêkotêk. The fragment preserves the plaque spelling exactly; an alternate normalized spelling for educational use would be nipêwin kâ kwâskwêkotêk kîkway or ...kîkwayak.
Syllabic transcription ᓂᐯᐃᐣ for 'nipêwin' uses the bare ᐃ for the medial 'wi' rather than the more standard ᐏ; the carved plaque appears to use the simpler vowel glyph. Flagged for elder review.
